articles.author: Vivek Yaligar
articles.description:
I built CompScan: a fully local system health tool that scans your machine, finds what's slowing you down, spots security issues, and fixes things with one command. Nothing ever leaves your computer.
Most "optimization" tools are either cloud-heavy, full of telemetry, or one-off scripts. I wanted one CLI that's private, cross-platform, and actually useful for developers.
Health check: CPU/RAM hogs, disk space, caches (often 2-15 GB reclaimable)
Security: SSH keys, credentials, firewall, permissions. Score out of 100.
Habits: late-night usage, marathon sessions, suggests breaks
One-click actions: cleanup caches, temp files, logs (trust-level gated)
Rust, ~3 MB binary, redb for storage, optional Ollama for deeper reasoning. macOS, Linux, Windows.
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vvk147/comp-scan/main/install.sh | bash

Or: cargo install --path . from the repo.
If you care about privacy and a fast machine, give it a try: github.com/vvk147/comp-scan
articles.title: CompScan: Your computer's health doctor. Fully local, private, free (Rust)

For years, I did what most developers do.
I put everything behind a cloud WAF.
It made sense:
change DNS
enable proxy
turn on a few managed rules
done
In under 10 minutes you get:
global CDN
DDoS protection
bot filtering
a Web Application Firewall
Platforms like Cloudflare make this incredibly easy. Their WAF runs on a massive global network and automatically blocks common attacks using managed rules and threat intelligence.
For most projects, this setup is more than enough.

Not all traffic fits well inside a cloud WAF model.
This post isn’t about abandoning cloud WAFs. I still use them heavily.

Every developer eventually encounters the infamous error:
Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com' from origin 'https://myapp.com'
has been blocked by CORS policy

At first glance, it feels like the server blocked your request.
But here’s the twist:
The request was not blocked.
refused to let your JavaScript read the response.
Understanding this single idea makes CORS far less mysterious.
Let's break it down step by step.
🟦 1. What is CORS?
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security rule.
It controls whether JavaScript running in the browser is allowed to read a response coming from another origin.
Important truths:
🚨 CORS is not a server security system

🚨 CORS does not block network requests

🚨 CORS is enforced only by browsers
